title: A vector is a move

text.guided:
A vector such as (2, 1) is not a place: it is a **move**. It says "go 2 to the right and 1 up". Put two moves one after the other, the start of the second on the tip of the first, and the ball lands on the **sum**.

To add vectors, add the x's together and the y's together. Always x first, then y.
text.fast: A vector is a displacement. $(a, b) + (c, d) = (a + c,\, b + d)$: add component by component, x first.

examples.games: A character takes two steps in a row: the total move is the sum of the two steps.
examples.physics: Two forces on a ball add up: the resulting force is the sum of the two vectors.
examples.sport: A one-two pass: (3, 1) then (1, 2) puts the ball at (4, 3) from where it started.

robot: Rule one of the Grid: a vector is a move, not a place. Watch the ball chain its shots.

mission.games: Your hero sits on (-1, -1) and the treasure is on (2, 1). Build the one move that gets there.
mission.physics: A puck rests at (-1, -1). Give it the one push that slides it onto (2, 1).
mission.sport: The ball is at (-1, -1) and your teammate waits at (2, 1). Pick the pass.

title: Flip it, stretch it

text.guided:
A minus sign turns a vector around: -(1, 1) is (-1, -1), the same length pointing the other way. A number in front of a vector stretches it: 2 × (-1, 1) = (-2, 2).

The number multiplies **both** coordinates, never only one.
text.fast: $k\,(x, y) = (kx,\, ky)$. A negative $k$ reverses the direction.

examples.games: Double speed doubles both the sideways and the upward part of your move.
examples.physics: Doubling a force doubles every component of it; reversing a force flips both signs.
examples.sport: Kick twice as hard: both the forward and the sideways part of the shot double. A back pass is a negative vector.

robot: Minus signs just mean the other way. Left and down are moves too.

mission.games: Retreat! Two moves take your hero from (2, 1) back to the safe spot (-2, 2).
mission.physics: Two pushes bring the puck from (2, 1) back to (-2, 2). Mind the signs.
mission.sport: Build the attack backwards: two passes from (2, 1) to the striker on (-2, 2).

title: Any order, same landing

text.guided:
Adding vectors does not care about the order: (2, 1) then (1, 2) lands on the same point as (1, 2) then (2, 1). The **path** is different, though, and a wall can block one path but not the other.

That is how you play around a wall: choose shots whose sum is the same, but whose path is clear.
text.fast: Vector addition is commutative: the landing point is the same in any order. Only the path changes, which matters when walls block it.

examples.games: Walk 3 east then 4 north, or 4 north then 3 east: you end on the same tile, but one route may cross a lava field.
examples.physics: The net displacement does not depend on the order of the legs of the trip.
examples.sport: Dribble 3 right then 4 up, or 4 up then 3 right: same spot, but one path may run into a defender.

robot: Order never changes where you land. It can change what you crash into, though.

check.prompt: Shots (2, 1) then (1, 2), compared with (1, 2) then (2, 1) from the same start. Where do the two balls end?
options: On the same point only if there is no wall
